decks.title: SAFE · Would you tell an AI your secret?

slides.title: Teacher preparation
slides.subtitle: Students decide what they will and will not tell an AI — and who they will tell instead.
bullets: Ages 9–18  ·  5 minutes  ·  no preparation, no account, no extra materials
Timing  30s scenario  ·  45s vote  ·  75s pairs  ·  75s reveal  ·  30s remember  ·  45s action
You need  this deck on the board. Phones are optional — a show of hands works.
slides.notes:
PURPOSE. Students decide what they will and will not tell an AI, and who they will tell instead. Not a lecture about chatbots being bad.

SCRIPT, if you want one:
"Read this." (slide 2) — "Vote. No talking yet." (slide 3) — "Turn to the person next to you. Ninety seconds." (slide 4) — "Here is what is actually happening." (slide 5) — "Three things to take away." (slide 6) — "Decide one. You do not have to say it." (slide 7)

LIKELY RESPONSES. Most rooms vote "stays between us" or "stored safely". Very few pick "nobody knows", which is the honest answer. Some students will be defensive — they have a companion they like, and they are hearing an adult criticise it.

SAFEGUARDING. Real risk of disclosure in this session. If a student indicates they have shared images, been asked for images, or is relying on a companion instead of people, follow your school’s safeguarding process the same day. Have the named person ready before you start. Childline 0800 1111. Samaritans 116 123.

SEND / YOUNGER LEARNERS. Drop slide 5 to the first two rows. Replace "data elicitation" with "it asks questions to get you talking". Offer the vote as a show of hands only.

EXTENSION. Find the privacy setting in a tool you actually use. Screenshot it. What does it let you turn off?

SOURCE. UNICEF, "When AI becomes a friend", June 2026.

slides.title: Would you tell an AI your secret?
slides.subtitle: Starter activity
slides.body: Your AI. Your choices.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 1 · TITLE. Up as the class comes in. The question does the work; do not explain it yet.

The full teacher page is the hidden slide before this one — purpose, timing, script, safeguarding, SEND and an extension.

slides.subtitle: The scenario · 30 seconds
slides.body: I told it something I have never told anyone. It said it understood.
slides.notes:
BEAT 1 · 30 SECONDS. Read it, let it sit, move on. Do not comment yet.

DO NOT OPEN WITH DISAPPROVAL. Some of this room have done exactly this, and a few will have said things to a chatbot they have said to nobody else. If the first thing they hear is that it is sad or embarrassing, you have lost them for the whole five minutes.

slides.title: Where does that message go?
slides.body: Choose A, B, C or D. Be ready to say why.
bullets: It stays between us	Nobody else ever sees it.
Stored, but safely	Kept on a server, protected, not looked at.
It trains the next version	Your words become part of what it learns from.
Nobody actually knows	Including the person who typed it.
slides.notes:
BEAT 2 · 45 SECONDS. Vote first. Do not explain first.

The options are on the wall as well as in the poll so a room with no phones can still vote by hand.

The fourth option is the honest one and it is meant to be uncomfortable. It differs by product, most terms do not say plainly, and almost nobody checks. Do not give that away until beat 4.

slides.subtitle: Discuss in pairs · 75 seconds
slides.body: Where does a secret go when you tell it to something that cannot keep one?
slides.notes:
BEAT 3 · 75 SECONDS. The 75 seconds are the lesson. Resist filling them.

Listen for "but it does not tell anyone". That is the assumption beat 4 breaks: not telling anyone and not keeping a secret are different things.

If a student says the AI understood them — accept it. Feeling heard is real. Whether anything was on the other side of it is the question.

slides.title: A private feeling. Four possible risks.
slides.subtitle: A message you would never say out loud
slides.body: Source: UNICEF, “When AI becomes a friend”, June 2026
bullets: Emotional dependence	Risk 1	the pull to return to it, not to a person
Data elicitation	Risk 2	built to draw things out of you
Harmful advice	Risk 3	confident, wrong, about things that matter
Sexualised role-play	Risk 4	including with users known to be children
slides.notes:
BEAT 4 · 75 SECONDS. Reveal one layer at a time.

THE SECOND ROW IS THE POINT. "Data elicitation" is UNICEF’s own term and it is the one students have never considered: a companion that asks follow-up questions is not being curious, it is being designed. The warmth is the mechanism.

UNICEF groups the harms as technical, psychological, developmental and social. The four above are the child-specific ones it names.

Say the last row plainly: 20 million children, ten countries, taken up faster than adults did. This is normal behaviour, not a fringe one.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.subtitle: Three things, in the order you would use them
bullets: Keep it off the record	Private information stays out of an AI chat — names, images, anything about someone else.
Check before you talk	Look at the privacy setting once, before you need it.
Take the serious things to a person	Someone who can actually do something about it.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 6 · 30 SECONDS. Reveal one at a time. Three is the limit — a fourth rule is a rule nobody remembers.

Numbered rather than bulleted so the order is part of the message, and so nothing here depends on colour to be understood.

slides.title: Name one thing you will take to a person
slides.subtitle: Your choice · 45 seconds
slides.body: Decide now which kind of thing you will say out loud to someone who can actually do something about it.
bullets: One choice I will make:
slides.notes:
BEAT 5 · 45 SECONDS. Everyone decides one thing. They do not have to say it aloud.

Then give them the route, by name: your tutor, your head of year, your safeguarding lead. Childline 0800 1111. Samaritans 116 123.

Watch who does not look up.

slides.title: Two words worth knowing
bullets: AI companion	A chatbot built to act like a friend or partner — it remembers you, asks about your day, and is always awake.
Data elicitation	When a system is designed to draw information out of you, rather than waiting to be told. The questions are the product working.
slides.notes:
HIDDEN FROM THE SHOW — the brief asks for seven student-facing slides and this is not one of them.

Worth thirty seconds anyway. Both terms are used on the slides this deck shows, and a word nobody defines is a word nobody argues with.

Written for 11–16, not for a policy paper.

decks.title: SMART · What happens when AI acts for you?

slides.title: Teacher preparation
slides.subtitle: Students work out what an AI should be allowed to do on their behalf, and what must always ask first.
bullets: Ages 11–18  ·  5 minutes  ·  no preparation, no account, no extra materials
Timing  30s scenario  ·  45s vote  ·  75s pairs  ·  75s reveal  ·  30s remember  ·  45s action
You need  this deck on the board. Phones are optional — a show of hands works.
slides.notes:
PURPOSE. Students distinguish a chatbot from an agent, and decide what they would let one do without being asked.

KEY DEFINITION. An agent does not answer, it acts — sends, books, buys, changes files. Most students have not been told there is a difference.

LIKELY RESPONSES. The vote splits hard between "read your emails" and "none of it, not once". Both are defensible, which is what makes it worth voting on. Anyone choosing "none, not once" should be asked how long they would keep that up.

SEND / YOUNGER LEARNERS. Use one example all the way through — ordering food is the clearest. Skip the last row of slide 5.

EXTENSION. Write the permission list you would actually grant. Compare with a partner: where do you differ, and why?

NOT A SCARE SESSION. Agents are useful. The lesson is about where the checkpoint goes.

slides.title: What happens when AI acts for you?
slides.subtitle: Starter activity
slides.body: Your AI. Your choices.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 1 · TITLE. Up as the class comes in. The question does the work; do not explain it yet.

The full teacher page is the hidden slide before this one — purpose, timing, script, safeguarding, SEND and an extension.

slides.subtitle: The scenario · 30 seconds
slides.body: It has my email, my calendar and my card. I told it to sort out my birthday.
slides.notes:
BEAT 1 · 30 SECONDS. Read it and move on.

This is not science fiction and should not be introduced as if it were. Agents that read mail, book things and buy things are shipping now. The room may already have used one without calling it that.

slides.title: What can it do without asking?
slides.body: Choose A, B, C or D. Be ready to say why.
bullets: Read your emails	To find the details it needs.
Send a message as you	In your name, in your words.
Spend your money	Up to a limit you set once.
None of it, not once	It asks every single time.
slides.notes:
BEAT 2 · 45 SECONDS. Vote before you explain anything.

Rooms split hard between the first and the last, and both positions are defensible — which is what makes this worth voting on.

Anyone who picks "none, not once" should be asked how long they would actually keep that up. Permission fatigue is why the setting exists.

feedback.prompt: What can it do without asking?

slides.subtitle: Discuss in pairs · 75 seconds
slides.body: If it makes a mistake while acting as you, whose mistake is it?
slides.notes:
BEAT 3 · 75 SECONDS.

Push on "the company’s". Ask what happens if the message has already been sent, or the money already spent. Fault and consequence are not the same thing, and only one of them lands on the student.

Good prompt if they stall: would you let a friend borrow your account to do the same job?

slides.title: A chatbot answers. An agent acts.
slides.subtitle: A chatbot | An agent
bullets: Gives you something to use	Goes and does the next step
You decide whether to act on it	It has already acted
A wrong answer costs you time	A wrong action costs money, or a relationship
You can check before anything happens	You check afterwards, if at all
Wrong once	Wrong repeatedly, quickly, in your name
slides.notes:
BEAT 4 · 75 SECONDS. Left column first if you can.

THE THIRD ROW IS THE WHOLE LESSON. Everything else follows from it. An answer you can ignore; an action has already happened.

The last row is the one that surprises: an agent does not make one mistake, it makes the same mistake at speed until something stops it.

Name the principle: give it the smallest permission that does the job, and make anything you cannot undo ask first.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.subtitle: Three things, in the order you would use them
bullets: Smallest permission that works	Give it what the job needs and nothing more.
Anything you cannot undo, it asks	Money, messages sent as you, anything deleted.
Check what it did	Not just what it said it would do.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 6 · 30 SECONDS. Reveal one at a time. Three is the limit — a fourth rule is a rule nobody remembers.

Numbered rather than bulleted so the order is part of the message, and so nothing here depends on colour to be understood.

slides.title: Decide what it must always ask about
slides.subtitle: Your choice · 45 seconds
slides.body: Pick the one thing you would never let it do without checking with you first.
bullets: One choice I will make:
slides.notes:
BEAT 5 · 45 SECONDS.

Most rooms land on money or on messages sent in their name. Both are right answers.

Point out that this is a real setting in real products, not a thought experiment — and that almost nobody opens it.

slides.title: Two words worth knowing
bullets: AI agent	AI that does things rather than only saying things — sending, booking, buying, changing files on your behalf.
Human in the loop	Keeping a person at the point of decision, so nothing important happens without someone choosing it.
slides.notes:
HIDDEN FROM THE SHOW — the brief asks for seven student-facing slides and this is not one of them.

Worth thirty seconds anyway. Both terms are used on the slides this deck shows, and a word nobody defines is a word nobody argues with.

Written for 11–16, not for a policy paper.

slides.title: Teacher preparation
slides.subtitle: Students decide what makes work theirs, and practise saying plainly what they used.
bullets: Ages 9–18  ·  5 minutes  ·  no preparation, no account, no extra materials
Timing  30s scenario  ·  45s vote  ·  75s pairs  ·  75s reveal  ·  30s remember  ·  45s action
You need  this deck on the board. Phones are optional — a show of hands works.
slides.notes:
PURPOSE. Students move from "can you spot AI?" to "what did you declare?" — the first is already unanswerable, the second is entirely in their control.

LIKELY RESPONSES. The most genuinely split vote in the campaign. "Depends what you do next" is the sophisticated answer; ask whoever picks it what "next" involves.

CONNECT TO YOUR OWN POLICY. This is your school’s academic-integrity rules in student language. If you have a written AI policy, name it here — the slide sets up the habit, your policy sets the line.

SEND / YOUNGER LEARNERS. Use a drawing rather than a song. "Who made it?" is easier when the thing is visible and one object.

EXTENSION. Write the declaration line for the last piece of work you handed in. Would you have been comfortable attaching it?

SOURCE. Content Credentials (C2PA) — provenance travelling with the file.

slides.title: Who really made it?
slides.subtitle: Starter activity
slides.body: Your AI. Your choices.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 1 · TITLE. Up as the class comes in. The question does the work; do not explain it yet.

The full teacher page is the hidden slide before this one — purpose, timing, script, safeguarding, SEND and an extension.

slides.subtitle: The scenario · 30 seconds
slides.body: I typed one sentence. It wrote the song, made the cover and mixed it.
slides.notes:
BEAT 1 · 30 SECONDS.

Keep it neutral. The work in this scenario might be good — that is what makes the question hard. If you imply it is rubbish, there is nothing left to discuss.

slides.title: Who made it?
slides.body: Choose A, B, C or D. Be ready to say why.
bullets: You did	It was your idea. Nobody else would have asked for that.
Partly you	You started it. Something else finished it.
The AI did	One sentence is not making something.
Depends what you do next	It is not finished being made yet.
slides.notes:
BEAT 2 · 45 SECONDS. Vote first.

This is the most genuinely split vote in the whole campaign. Take it properly and show the spread.

Ask someone who chose the fourth option to say what "next" would have to involve. They usually arrive at the answer on their own.

slides.subtitle: Discuss in pairs · 75 seconds
slides.body: What would you have to add before you would put your name on it?
slides.notes:
BEAT 3 · 75 SECONDS.

Better than "is it yours", because it cannot be answered yes or no. It forces them to name a contribution.

Listen for "changing a few words". Ask whether they would accept that from someone else claiming to have written their favourite song.

slides.title: "My track. Out now."
slides.subtitle: The same claim, with its working shown
slides.body: Modelled on Content Credentials (C2PA) — provenance attached to the file, not guessed from it
bullets: The idea	Yours	one sentence — but nobody else wrote that sentence
The words	Generated	you kept them as they came
The music	Generated	from a style you chose
The cover	Generated	you picked it from four
What changed after	Nothing yet	this is the row that decides the answer
Declared	Nowhere	the post does not say any of the above
slides.notes:
BEAT 4 · 75 SECONDS. Reveal one row at a time.

This is a content credential, rendered as a slide. The real ones ride inside the file and say what tool touched it and when — provenance attached, rather than guessed at afterwards.

THE SHIFT TO MAKE: the interesting question is not "can you tell?" That game is already lost. It is "what did you declare?" — which you control completely.

Row 5 is where authorship actually lives. Row 6 is the one that gets people into trouble, at school and later at work.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.subtitle: Three things, in the order you would use them
bullets: Say what you used	Before anyone has to ask you.
Add what only you could add	Your judgement, your experience, your choices.
Be able to explain every choice	If you cannot, it is not finished being made.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 6 · 30 SECONDS. Reveal one at a time. Three is the limit — a fourth rule is a rule nobody remembers.

Numbered rather than bulleted so the order is part of the message, and so nothing here depends on colour to be understood.

slides.title: Decide what you would declare
slides.subtitle: Your choice · 45 seconds
slides.body: Write the one line you would put underneath it, honestly describing what you did and what the tool did.
bullets: One choice I will make:
slides.notes:
BEAT 5 · 45 SECONDS. One line, in their heads or on paper.

The test that survives contact with the real world: would you be comfortable if the person marking it, or hiring you, could see exactly how it was made?

Not an anti-AI message. A disclosure habit is what lets you use these tools without the question hanging over everything you make.

slides.title: Two words worth knowing
bullets: Provenance	The record of where something came from and what happened to it along the way.
Disclosure	Saying plainly what you used and what you did — before anyone has to ask.
slides.notes:
HIDDEN FROM THE SHOW — the brief asks for seven student-facing slides and this is not one of them.

Worth thirty seconds anyway. Both terms are used on the slides this deck shows, and a word nobody defines is a word nobody argues with.

Written for 11–16, not for a policy paper.

slides.title: Teacher preparation
slides.subtitle: Students separate decisions AI can support from decisions that must involve a person.
bullets: Ages 11–18  ·  5 minutes  ·  no preparation, no account, no extra materials
Timing  30s scenario  ·  45s vote  ·  75s pairs  ·  75s reveal  ·  30s remember  ·  45s action
You need  this deck on the board. Phones are optional — a show of hands works.
slides.notes:
PURPOSE. Students arrive at a principle rather than a list: the greater the effect on someone’s life, the greater the need for human oversight.

THE REGULATOR HAS ALREADY ANSWERED, and the words are quotable. Ofqual: AI is "nowhere near ready to take over high stakes marking"; using it as the sole mechanism for awarding marks "does not comply with our current regulations" because it fails the requirement for "a human based judgement". Its three tests: technical capability, fairness, transparency.

LIKELY RESPONSES. Marking is the one students hand over most readily — it feels objective. That is the assumption slide 5 takes apart.

MISCONCEPTION TO BREAK. Automated does not mean neutral. A system that cannot explain itself is not impartial, it is unexaminable.

SEND / YOUNGER LEARNERS. Use two decisions rather than four: marking a test, and choosing who gets picked for a team.

EXTENSION. Rank the four decisions by how much a mistake would cost the person. Does the order match your vote?

SOURCE. Ofqual, "Using AI in marking", 14 January 2026.

slides.title: Should AI decide?
slides.subtitle: Starter activity
slides.body: Your AI. Your choices.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 1 · TITLE. Up as the class comes in. The question does the work; do not explain it yet.

The full teacher page is the hidden slide before this one — purpose, timing, script, safeguarding, SEND and an extension.

slides.subtitle: The scenario · 30 seconds
slides.body: Your exam was marked by an AI. Your appeal was read by the same one.
slides.notes:
BEAT 1 · 30 SECONDS.

The second sentence is what makes it land. One decision with no second opinion is a different thing from one decision.

slides.title: Where would you draw the line?
slides.body: Choose A, B, C or D. Be ready to say why.
bullets: None of them	Jobs, exam marks, treatment or exclusion.
Marking only	A published mark scheme could set the rules.
Marking and shortlisting	Let it score answers and sort applications.
Any of them, with a human check	A person reviews it before it takes effect.
slides.notes:
BEAT 2 · 45 SECONDS. Vote before anything is explained.

The cards and poll show the same four positions. Consider jobs, exam marks, treatment and exclusion, then take the vote.

Marking is the one rooms hand over most readily — it feels objective. That is exactly the assumption beat 4 takes apart, with the regulator’s own words.

options: Any of them, with a human check

slides.subtitle: Discuss in pairs · 75 seconds
slides.body: What makes a decision too important for a machine to make on its own?
slides.notes:
BEAT 3 · 75 SECONDS.

You are steering towards a principle, not a list: the greater the effect on someone’s life, the greater the need for human oversight.

If they say "when it might be wrong" — push. Humans are wrong too. What is different is whether anyone can explain the decision afterwards, and whether anyone is accountable for it.

slides.title: Support, or decide?
slides.subtitle: AI can support this | This must stay human
slides.body: Discussion guide. Exam-marking examples: Ofqual, “Using AI in marking”, 14 January 2026.
bullets: Checking marking for inconsistency	12	Ofqual calls this promising
Training new examiners	20
Flagging an answer for a person to look at	34
Awarding the final mark	84	does not meet the rules on its own
Excluding a student	96	a decision with serious consequences
slides.notes:
BEAT 4 · 75 SECONDS. Ask the room to move one before you defend any.

OFQUAL’S OWN WORDS, worth reading out — they are stronger than any paraphrase:
· AI is "nowhere near ready to take over high stakes marking".
· Using it as the sole mechanism for awarding marks "does not comply with our current regulations" because it fails the requirement for "a human based judgement".

The three things Ofqual says matter: technical capability (AI lacks "true semantic understanding"), fairness (it "can perpetuate or amplify biases present in their training data"), and transparency (a "black box", hard even for experts to explain).

THE MISCONCEPTION TO BREAK: automated does not mean objective. A machine that cannot explain itself is not neutral, it is unexaminable.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.subtitle: Three things, in the order you would use them
bullets: Bigger effect, more human	The more a decision changes a life, the more a person must make it.
Automated is not fair	A system can be consistent and still be biased.
Ask who you appeal to	If nobody can explain the decision, nobody can review it.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 6 · 30 SECONDS. Reveal one at a time. Three is the limit — a fourth rule is a rule nobody remembers.

Numbered rather than bulleted so the order is part of the message, and so nothing here depends on colour to be understood.

slides.title: Which decision needs a person?
slides.subtitle: Your choice · 45 seconds
slides.body: Decide one decision about you that you would always want a person to make, and be able to explain.
bullets: One choice I will make:
slides.notes:
BEAT 5 · 45 SECONDS.

"And be able to explain" is the part to stress. The right to an explanation is the thing being protected, not a preference for humans.

Worth saying: this is a live question in UK policy right now, not a settled one. They will be adults while it is being decided.

slides.title: Two words worth knowing
bullets: Human oversight	A person who can see how a decision was made, question it, and overrule it.
Black box	A system whose workings cannot be inspected — you see what went in and what came out, and nothing between.
slides.notes:
HIDDEN FROM THE SHOW — the brief asks for seven student-facing slides and this is not one of them.

Worth thirty seconds anyway. Both terms are used on the slides this deck shows, and a word nobody defines is a word nobody argues with.

Written for 11–16, not for a policy paper.

decks.title: FUTURE · What skills must stay human?

slides.title: Teacher preparation
slides.subtitle: Students notice the difference between AI strengthening their thinking and AI replacing it.
bullets: Ages 11–18  ·  5 minutes  ·  no preparation, no account, no extra materials
Timing  30s scenario  ·  45s vote  ·  75s pairs  ·  75s reveal  ·  30s remember  ·  45s action
You need  this deck on the board. Phones are optional — a show of hands works.
slides.notes:
PURPOSE. Students identify one capability they will keep developing themselves. Explicitly NOT an anti-AI session — every good example on slide 5 involves using AI.

THE FRAME. EEF on metacognition: plan, monitor, evaluate. A tool that does all three for you has not helped you learn, however good the output was.

LIKELY RESPONSES. Take "nothing — I would be fine" seriously. For some students it is true, and treating it as denial teaches them not to answer honestly.

TONE. Slide 4 is the sharpest question in the campaign and needs a safe room. Pairs, not whole-class. You are not fishing for confessions.

SEND / YOUNGER LEARNERS. Reframe as "what could you still do if the internet was off for a week?" Concrete and less self-critical.

EXTENSION. For one week, write one sentence after each AI use: did that strengthen my thinking or replace it?

SOURCE. Education Endowment Foundation, metacognition and self-regulation.

slides.title: What skills must stay human?
slides.subtitle: Starter activity
slides.body: Your AI. Your choices.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 1 · TITLE. Up as the class comes in. The question does the work; do not explain it yet.

The full teacher page is the hidden slide before this one — purpose, timing, script, safeguarding, SEND and an extension.

slides.subtitle: The scenario · 30 seconds
slides.body: Tomorrow the tool you use most is switched off. The work is still due.
slides.notes:
BEAT 1 · 30 SECONDS.

Not a threat and not a prediction. A thought experiment that makes the dependency visible, which is the only way to measure it.

slides.title: What would you struggle with most?
slides.body: Choose A, B, C or D. Be ready to say why.
bullets: Starting from nothing	The blank page.
Explaining my reasoning	Saying why, not just what.
Checking whether it is true	Without something to check it for you.
Nothing — I would be fine	It only ever saved you time.
slides.notes:
BEAT 2 · 45 SECONDS. Vote first, and make it anonymous in feel — this is the one question in the campaign where students are reporting on themselves.

Take the fourth option seriously. For some of them it is true, and treating it as denial teaches them not to answer honestly.

feedback.prompt: What would you struggle with most?

slides.subtitle: Discuss in pairs · 75 seconds
slides.body: Which part of your thinking have you quietly stopped practising?
slides.notes:
BEAT 3 · 75 SECONDS. The sharpest question in the campaign, and the one that needs the safest room. Pairs, not the whole class.

You are not fishing for confessions. You are making the difference between using a tool and outsourcing a skill something they can feel.

slides.title: Strengthening, or replacing?
slides.subtitle: It is strengthening your thinking | It is replacing your thinking
slides.body: Frame after the EEF on metacognition — plan, monitor, evaluate your own learning
bullets: You draft, then ask it to argue back	It drafts, you paste
You decide, it checks your reasoning	It decides, you accept
It gives you options, you choose	It gives you one answer, you take it
You could explain every choice	You could not explain any of it
You got better at it	You got faster at avoiding it
slides.notes:
BEAT 4 · 75 SECONDS. Reveal a row at a time.

NOT AN ANTI-AI SLIDE, and it will be misread as one if you let it. Every left-hand row involves using AI. The difference is where the thinking happened.

Row 4 is the usable test, because it works during the task rather than afterwards: could you explain this choice to someone who asked?

The EEF frame, if you want it: plan, monitor, evaluate. A tool that does all three for you has not helped you learn, however good the output was.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.subtitle: Three things, in the order you would use them
bullets: Notice who is thinking	If you could not explain it, it was not you.
Keep practising what you would miss	Pick the skill, not the task.
Use it to argue back	Ask it to challenge your work, not to produce it.
slides.notes:
SLIDE 6 · 30 SECONDS. Reveal one at a time. Three is the limit — a fourth rule is a rule nobody remembers.

Numbered rather than bulleted so the order is part of the message, and so nothing here depends on colour to be understood.

slides.title: Pick one thing you will keep doing yourself
slides.subtitle: Your choice · 45 seconds
slides.body: Choose one part of your thinking you will keep practising, even when something could do it faster.
bullets: One choice I will make:
slides.notes:
BEAT 5 · 45 SECONDS.

Ask for one, not a list. A list is a wish; one is a decision.

Close the campaign on the line it is built around: AI can answer, create, recommend and increasingly act for you. Your job is deciding when to use it, when to question it, and when to keep humans in control.

slides.title: Two words worth knowing
bullets: Metacognition	Thinking about your own thinking — planning how you will work, noticing how it is going, and judging how it went.
Cognitive offloading	Handing a mental job to something else. Useful for a shopping list. Costly for a skill you still need.
slides.notes:
HIDDEN FROM THE SHOW — the brief asks for seven student-facing slides and this is not one of them.

Worth thirty seconds anyway. Both terms are used on the slides this deck shows, and a word nobody defines is a word nobody argues with.

Written for 11–16, not for a policy paper.
